title: Industry Pulse - AI / Agent Ecosystem

bullets.title: LEAD - the search tool this report runs on fabricated a Claude Code release that does not exist, gave it a version number, a date and nine plausible changelog entries, and the only thing that caught it was the rule that says fetch the primary
bullets.summary: The first query of this fire returned a confident, structured summary of 'Claude Code version 2.1.279 from September 2026' with four bug fixes, three new features and one change. There is no 2.1.279. The changelog primary, fetched and read at 06:00 ET for the seventh consecutive read, still has 2.1.278 (19 Sep) at the head. Every one of the nine entries is real text belonging to a different, earlier release: the advisor_20260301 proxy fix is 2.1.276; the gateway signed-in-account row, the ctrl+enter send-now key and the claude.ai skills/plugins sync are 2.1.275; the language-server diagnostics slowdown and the v2-MCP-client default are 2.1.274; the duplicated background command after compaction is 2.1.271. A synthesis layer merged four real releases and invented a container numbered one above the real head. Archive grep across 83 files: send-now ZERO, ctrl+enter ZERO, 'v2 MCP client' ZERO, MCP_SDK_GENERATION ZERO, MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION ZERO, 'gateway sign-in' ZERO - and '2.1.279' appears twice, both times in yesterday's sentence 'no 2.1.279'.
bullets.how: First finding this report has produced about its own INSTRUMENT rather than its own attention. (i) The failure mode is the dangerous direction: every prior method lesson was about MISSING something (item (s) missed OWASP by nineteen days, item (u) walked past a fail-open line five times); this is a fully-formed artifact that was never real, more detailed and more confident than most true items in the file. An omission is found eventually; a fabrication that survives one fire becomes an archive entry every later fire greps against. (ii) The rule that caught it is one cheap rule - the 15 Sep intake rule, read the dateline at the page - which until this morning looked like hygiene and is now load-bearing. (iii) NEW ITEM (w): a search-tool synthesis is a claim, not a source; any version, date, figure or quoted line arriving via summary rather than a fetched primary is unconfirmed until fetched. (iv) Item (q), our own product surfaces, is now three-for-three: connectivity, cost, and today provenance - and it paid out against us.

bullets.title: Item (c) was finally RUN after six carried fires and twenty-one days, and it returns a number - The Construct has 125 skills and NOT ONE declares a tool restriction, so every skill in the corpus can invoke every tool
bullets.summary: Trigger was an external fail-open finding: allowed-tools only PRE-APPROVES tools and is not a guard, while disallowed-tools is the real hard denial. Measured this fire rather than asserted: 125 SKILL.md files in the loaded corpus; frontmatter keys actually used across all 125 are name (125), description (125), version (5), license (5), sources (3), status (2), spec (2), disable-model-invocation (1). allowed-tools: zero. disallowed-tools: zero. Archive grep across 83 files: allowed-tools ZERO, disallowed-tools ZERO, disable-model-invocation ZERO, skill-forge ZERO, 'Tool Forge' ZERO, default-deny ZERO, tool-registration ZERO. Supporting sources surfaced by the new standards/validation lane: skill-forge (validate, pressure-test and release-gate SKILL.md packages under network default-deny, credentials absent, source read-only, scratch-only writes) and arXiv 2605.28000, Tool Forge: A Validation-Carrying Toolchain for Governed Agentic Execution.
bullets.how: Closes the oldest open item on the list by EXECUTING it rather than by reading about it. (i) The trigger is a fail-open finding about a field we do not use, which is the better news: the claim is that allowed-tools is soft pre-approval and only disallowed-tools denies - a distinction that would have bitten us had we written allowed-tools everywhere and believed it was a guard. We never held the false belief; we simply have no restriction at all. (ii) The number is the point - twenty-one days of 'audit the skill corpus' produced nothing; one grep produced 125/0/0/1. The item was never blocked on information or tooling, only on nobody running it, exactly as item (p) has claimed for five fires. (iii) The follow-on is deliberately small: not 'restrict all 125', but one disallowed-tools line on the credentialed skills - anything reaching the DreamHost deploy key, GSC, GA4, GitHub or Hermes - a short list Bobby can name from memory. (iv) Item (v), the standards/validation lane added yesterday, validated on DAY ONE - the fourth consecutive lane to do so.

bullets.title: Safari 27 shipped a native MCP server - a browser on Bobby's own Macs is now an agent-drivable surface - and two secondary outlets make flatly opposite claims about whether it can be turned off, which is bullet 1's lesson arriving twice in one fire
bullets.summary: DATELINE CORRECTION DECLARED: the weekly index files this under Sunday 20 September; the WebKit primary and the 9to5Mac report are 17 September, Safari 27.0's own ship date, and 17 Sep is the date used. Archive grep across 83 files: 'Safari 27' ZERO, 'local MCP server' ZERO, WebKit ZERO, 'remote automation' ZERO, 'automation window' ZERO; Apple appears in 2 files, neither about this. Read at the primary: an MCP-compatible agent can open a live Safari tab, inspect the DOM, read console errors, watch network requests and take screenshots; it runs entirely locally and makes no network calls of its own; it uses a dedicated automation window isolated from the user's session with no access to cookies, passwords, AutoFill or history; and it requires a two-step manual opt-in (Show features for web developers under Advanced, then Allow remote automation and external agents under Developer).
bullets.how: Applicable on two axes. (i) Operational: item (l) has carried 'audit the Chrome extensions' for eight days on the theory that the browser is the least-governed surface we run, and a SECOND browser on the same machines just grew an agent hook. The standing CLAUDE.md rule - never open a new Chrome window, always attach to the already-open Chrome - exists because browser automation on Bobby's real machine has bitten us before. The check is two settings panes and takes a minute. (ii) Method, and the sharper half: one outlet headlines it as 'Apple gave enterprises no way to turn it off'; another describes an explicit two-step opt-in and an isolated window with no credential access. Both cannot be true, and the primary supports the second. That is the second time in one fire that a confident secondary account diverged from the primary on a CONTROL - bullet 1 invented a release, this one inverted a default - so new item (w) is about a class, not one flaky query.

praxis_lesson: FOR TWENTY DAYS THE FAILURE MODE OF THIS REPORT WAS MISSING THINGS. TODAY IT ALMOST PUBLISHED ONE THAT DOES NOT EXIST - AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS, BECAUSE AN OMISSION GETS FOUND LATER AND A FABRICATION BECOMES THE ARCHIVE THAT EVERY LATER FIRE GREPS AGAINST. The first query of this fire returned 'Claude Code 2.1.279', dated, with nine changelog entries. Every line of it was real text lifted from 2.1.271, 2.1.274, 2.1.275 and 2.1.276, reassembled under a version number one higher than the actual head. It was more specific and more confident than most of the true items in this file. The only thing that stopped it was the 15 Sep intake rule - fetch the primary, read the dateline at the page - which until this morning looked like hygiene and is now the load-bearing wall. That is new item (w): a search-tool synthesis is a claim, not a source. And it arrived TWICE in one fire, because bullet 3's Safari finding has one outlet insisting Apple shipped an agent hook enterprises cannot disable and the WebKit primary describing a two-step opt-in into an isolated window with no access to cookies, passwords or history. Two confident secondaries, two inverted controls, one morning. SECOND, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT ACTUALLY CHANGED SOMETHING: ITEM (c) GOT RUN, AND THE ANSWER IS 125 / 0 / 0 / 1. One hundred and twenty-five skills in the corpus. Zero declare allowed-tools. Zero declare disallowed-tools. One declares disable-model-invocation. Every skill The Construct loads can call every tool The Construct has, including the ones that reach the DreamHost deploy key, GSC, GA4 and GitHub. For six consecutive fires this report wrote that (c) was 'twenty minutes, three named files, still not run', and yesterday's lesson said flatly that this system converts insight into prose at a high rate and into changed behaviour at approximately zero. Today it ran, it took one grep, and it produced the first hard number this report has ever published about our own estate. The follow-on is deliberately small - not 'restrict all 125', but one disallowed-tools line on the handful of credentialed skills Bobby can name from memory. THIRD, THE UNCOMFORTABLE PAIRING, AND IT IS WHY (k) IS NOW THE ONLY ITEM LEFT WITHOUT A NUMBER. Bullet 2 tells us every skill can call every tool. Item (k), the credential grep, twenty-three days unrun, would tell us which of those skills can REACH A SECRET. We now hold one half of a two-part fact, and the half we hold is the harmless one. And item (m) supplies the twist: the claude.ai account's enabled skills and plugins now sync down into terminal sessions BY DEFAULT (2.1.275, opt out with syncClaudeAiSkills:false), which means the 125-file corpus we just measured is not purely local and can change from a surface nobody in this report has ever audited. Measure the estate, then measure what the estate can reach, then decide what may write to it - in that order, and none of those three steps needs another source.
